answers.answer:
They share a family because SCOPe classifies TAL effector proteins as a single domain built from a variable number of the same ~34-residue repeat, and the family-level grouping is based on homology of the repeating unit, not on total length. In SCOPe 2.08 all three SIDs have the identical lineage: class a (all alpha proteins, sunid 46456) > fold a.298 'Left-handed alpha-alpha superhelix' (sunid 267589) > superfamily a.298.1 'TAL effector-like' (sunid 267596) > family a.298.1.1 'TAL (transcription activator-like) effector' (sunid 267609). They differ only at the protein and species levels: d2kq5a_ is PthA from Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. citri, d3v6pa_ is dHax3 from Xanthomonas, and d4cj9a_ is BurrH from Burkholderia rhizoxinica.

Length data (SEQRES, genetic style, release 2.08): d2kq5a_ = 51 residues, d3v6pa_ = 373 residues, d4cj9a_ = 752 residues. The ~15-fold length range reflects repeat copy number. d2kq5a_ carries the explicit SCOPe comment 'single repeat' (an NMR structure of one and a half TAL repeats, PDB 2kq5). d3v6pa_ (PDB 3v6p, a designed dHax3 construct) contains roughly 11 copies of the ~34-residue repeat visible in its sequence (the recurring '...LTPEQVVAIAS..GGKQALETVQRLLPVLCQAHG' motif). d4cj9a_ (PDB 4cj9, the BurrH TALE-like protein) contains roughly 20 or more copies of a homologous but more divergent repeat. SCOPe records the canonical repeat unit for the family as 4cj9 A:259-292, i.e. a 34-residue unit, with d4cj9a_ as the repeat representative.

SCOPe handles this explicitly through its 'different number of repeats' annotation. Both d2kq5a_ and d3v6pa_ carry the inconsistency flag 're', defined as 'applies to all domains of a family if the common domain is composed of a different number of small repeating units'. This is the formal statement that whole-chain domains in this family are expected to differ in size by integer multiples of the repeat. The reason the repeats are not split into separate SCOPe domains is that an individual 34-residue two-helix repeat is not an independently folding globular unit; the biologically meaningful structural unit is the superhelical array, so SCOPe treats the whole repeat array as one domain, consistent with how it classifies other solenoid folds. Consequently, domain length is not a classification criterion here.

Evolutionary-strength interpretation: membership in the same family (a.298.1.1) asserts clear homology, typically supported by significant sequence similarity of the repeat units, which is evident for the two Xanthomonas TALEs and extends to Burkholderia BurrH despite its lower per-repeat identity. The superfamily level (a.298.1) would assert homology on structural and functional grounds even without strong sequence similarity, and the fold level (a.298, left-handed alpha-alpha superhelix) asserts only shared topology, which by itself is not evidence of homology. Here all three agree down to family, so homology is well supported. Important limits: shared family does not imply identical repeat count, identical repeat sequence, or interchangeable function; functional details such as the repeat-variable positions and what each individual repeat contacts should not be transferred between PthA, dHax3 and BurrH without their own sequence-level and structural evidence. The 51-residue d2kq5a_ fragment is not a representative of the full superhelical architecture and is a poor template for whole-protein modelling, whereas d4cj9a_ (the longest and the designated repeat representative) is the better structural representative of the family. Sequence-alignment coverage statistics between these domains will be misleading because of the length disparity, and any comparison should be done at the level of individual repeats rather than whole domains.
